Public Law Update – Tax Measure Amending the California Constitution on the November Ballot
Aug 18, 2026
Introduction
As a result of a compromise between Governor Newsom’s office and the proponents for two sweeping tax measures, only one local-tax measure will be on the November 2026 ballot — Proposition 43 (ACA 22). If approved by the voters, it will require a two-thirds vote for citizen-initiated special taxes going forward, effective January 1, 2027, without disturbing taxes voters have already approved. Two more sweeping measures — Initiative 1983 and ACA 13 — were withdrawn in the last-minute deal, and an earlier, broader initiative had already been struck down in court.
This update walks through each piece: what qualified, what was removed, and the negotiations and court ruling that explain why.
The background — why local taxes became a fight
To understand what was pulled and why, it helps to know the underlying dispute.
Under Proposition 13, special taxes generally need a two-thirds vote to pass. But in 2017, California courts ruled that when a tax measure is put on the ballot by citizens through the initiative process — rather than by a city council or other government body — it only needs a simple majority (over 50%). California Cannabis Coal. v. City of Upland (2017) 3 Cal. 5th 924. This allows tax increase proponents to bypass the constitutional two-thirds requirement.
What didn’t make the ballot — and why
A. Initiative 1983 — withdrawn through the negotiated deal
Initiative 1983 (petition 25-0006A1, Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13), backed by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, would have been the most far-reaching. It would have:
Raised the approval threshold for voter-initiated tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds;
Applied to all local governments, including charter cities, and barred them — and voters exercising the initiative power — from imposing real property transfer, sales, or documentary taxes above the rate set by Revenue and Taxation Code section 11911 as it existed on January 1, 2025 (the roughly 0.11% state baseline), while also restricting ad valorem and non-ad valorem taxes on real property; and
Applied retroactively, providing that non-compliant property-related taxes enacted before its effective date would become null and void on December 31 of the second year following enactment — by December 31, 2028, assuming a 2026 effective date.
That retroactive feature is what alarmed local governments — it put already-approved local taxes at risk of being invalidated.
B. ACA 13 — removed as part of the same deal
ACA 13 (Ward), proposed by the Legislature, would have required that any initiative seeking to raise the voter-approval threshold to adopt any state or local measure — not just tax measures — itself pass by that same higher threshold, and it applied to statewide initiatives appearing on the ballot on or after January 1, 2024. The measure, titled the Protect and Retain the Majority Vote Act, also authorized local governing bodies to hold non-binding advisory votes on issues of governance. In practice, its threshold rule meant the Jarvis measure would have needed two-thirds support to pass.
C. The compromise: both pulled, replaced by ACA 22 (now Proposition 43)
Just before the June 25, 2026 deadline for measures to qualify or be removed, the proponents of Initiative 1983, Governor Gavin Newsom, and legislative leaders announced a deal. Under the deal, Initiative 1983 and ACA 13 were both removed from the November ballot, and they were replaced by ACA 22 (Wicks) — now Proposition 43.
If voters approve it by majority vote, (Cal. Const. art XVIII sec. 4), ACA 22 (Proposition 43) would increase the vote threshold for special taxes placed on the ballot by citizens’ initiative from a simple majority to a two-thirds supermajority — but only going forward, starting January 1, 2027. Crucially, it applies prospectively only: local ballot measures approved on or before the November 2026 election are no longer at risk of being invalidated.
ACA 22 (Proposition 43) writes a new Section 4.5 into Article XIII A of the California Constitution (the article Proposition 13 created). The compromise gives each side part of what it wanted. Prop 13 supporters get a higher, constitutionally fixed threshold for future citizen-initiative tax measures; local governments keep the taxes their voters have already approved. Voters now decide only the narrower, forward-looking question rather than the sweeping retroactive one.
The measure reads, in its entirety:
Resolved by the Assembly, the Senate concurring, That the Legislature of the State of California at its 2025–26 Regular Session commencing on the second day of December 2024, two-thirds of the membership of each house concurring, hereby proposes to the people of the State of California, that the Constitution of the State be amended as follows:
That Section 4.5 is added to Article XIIIA thereof, to read:
SEC. 4.5. (a) Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIIIC, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIIID, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.
(b) Notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIIID.
(c) “Local government” and “special tax” shall have the same meaning as provided in Section 1 of Article XIIIC.
What to watch going forward
For public agencies, the practical upshot is stability. Assuming Proposition 43 passes, local special taxes and property-related taxes approved by voters on or before November 2026 remain valid as the initiative reaches only measures going forward. Organizers of future citizen initiatives seeking local special taxes would need to clear a two-thirds supermajority rather than a simple majority, and citizen-initiated ad valorem real-property taxes are barred outright — both effective January 1, 2027. Because the measure operates prospectively, timing matters: local tax measures on the November 2026 ballot are still governed by the current majority-vote rule, while later efforts would face the higher threshold if voters adopt Proposition 43. We will continue to monitor the election results and any subsequent litigation or implementing legislation.

Quick Facts
​​​​​​ Official ballot title: “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
Type: Legislative constitutional amendment (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, Resolution Chapter 132, filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
A vote YES means: New, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters through the initiative power would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same threshold already required when a city council or county board places a special tax on the ballot. Local governments and their voters also could not impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the limits already in the state constitution.
A vote NO means: Certain local special taxes could continue to be approved by a simple majority vote when placed on the ballot by citizen initiative.
Sponsor/proponent: Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22 as a legislative compromise. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association drove the underlying policy and its qualified citizen initiative.
On the ballot because: The legislature placed it on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house on June 25, 2026, as a compromise. In exchange, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew its already-qualified initiative (AG No. 25-0006A1).
Full legal text: ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 43 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 43 would raise the vote threshold for one specific path to a new local tax. Today, when a city council or county board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax, meaning a tax earmarked for a specific purpose, that tax needs a two-thirds vote to pass. That requirement traces to Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996. A separate path exists. When voters themselves place a special tax on the ballot through the citizen initiative, a series of court decisions has allowed that tax to pass with a simple majority. Proposition 43 would close that gap. Beginning January 1, 2027, a voter-initiated local special tax would need the same two-thirds vote as a government-sponsored one.
The measure carries a second provision that has drawn less attention. It also bars a local government, including its electorate acting by initiative, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property beyond the 1 percent rate that Proposition 13 already allows. This extends the existing constitutional limit so that it cannot be worked around through the initiative power.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office frames the practical effect plainly. By raising the bar for these taxes, the measure makes it harder for local governments to raise certain revenues, so local tax collections could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The office adds that the actual impact is unknown and would depend on future choices by voters and local officials.
2. The legal language
Full text: ACA 22, “Local Taxes: Limitation,” Resolution Chapter 132, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) (filed with the secretary of state June 25, 2026)
Key language:
“Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.” [1, Sec. 4.5(a)]
What it amends: Adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own. The phrase “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power” is the operative change, since it applies the two-thirds requirement to citizen initiatives, which recent court rulings had exempted.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland) authored ACA 22, but she did so as the vehicle for a negotiated deal rather than as a personal cause, and she has since said she opposes the measure. The policy behind it belongs to the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and its president, Jon Coupal, who had qualified a broader citizen initiative and agreed to pull it once the legislature placed this narrower version on the ballot. Opposition comes from transit, housing, and local government advocates who rely on majority-vote initiatives to fund services.
What? A two-thirds vote requirement for voter-initiated local special taxes, plus a bar on using the initiative power to impose ad valorem property taxes beyond the existing 1 percent limit.
Where? Statewide in effect, but it governs local taxes, so its bite is felt in the cities, counties, and special districts where citizen tax initiatives appear.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. The requirement applies to taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
Why? Supporters argue that a special tax is a special tax no matter who puts it on the ballot, and that letting initiatives pass earmarked taxes by a simple majority is an end run around a taxpayer protection that has stood since Proposition 13. Opponents argue that the citizen initiative is a core democratic tool and that a supermajority requirement lets a minority of voters block services the majority wants.
4. Trade-offs
For roughly two decades after Proposition 218, most people assumed every local special tax needed two-thirds approval. The California Supreme Court unsettled that assumption in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017), holding that the procedural limits Proposition 218 placed on local governments do not automatically bind voters acting through the initiative. The court itself called the change modest and left the two-thirds question open. Lower courts then took the next step, upholding several citizen special taxes that had passed with a majority rather than a two-thirds vote. That line of cases is what Proposition 43 would overturn.
The trade-off is real on both sides. The measure closes what supporters see as a loophole that lets organized campaigns pass targeted taxes with less consensus than the state constitution otherwise demands. A two-thirds rule protects the minority who bear the tax, and it forces broad agreement before money is committed to a single purpose. But the same rule is a powerful brake. Supermajority requirements let roughly one-third of voters defeat what a majority supports, and the taxes that have passed by majority under the current rule are not abstractions. They have funded things like fire protection, health services, and open-space preservation in specific counties. Under Proposition 43 several of those recent measures would have failed despite winning majority support.
There is also a worthwhile point about scope. Proposition 43 is deliberately narrower than the initiative it replaced. The original Howard Jarvis measure would also have restricted certain charter-city real estate transfer taxes and would have reached backward to invalidate some taxes already in place. ACA 22 drops both of those features and applies only going forward. Voters weighing this measure are voting on the prospective threshold change and the ad valorem limit, not on the more sweeping version that was withdrawn.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It restores a single, consistent rule. A local special tax would need two-thirds approval regardless of whether a city council or a citizen initiative places it on the ballot, ending a distinction that turned on procedure rather than substance.
It strengthens a long-standing taxpayer protection. The two-thirds requirement for earmarked local taxes has been part of California law since Proposition 13 and Proposition 218, and the measure keeps the initiative power from bypassing it.
It is prospective and narrow. Unlike the withdrawn initiative, it does not invalidate existing taxes or add new limits on real estate transfer taxes, which reduces the risk of disruptively unwinding revenue already budgeted.
It adds certainty. Litigation since Upland left the majority-versus-two-thirds question unsettled for years, and a clear constitutional rule would end that ambiguity.
Potential risks
It makes it harder to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst finds local tax revenues could be lower than they otherwise would be, though the size of the effect is unknown.
It lets a minority block a majority. A tax with 60 percent support would fail, so about one-third of voters could defeat a measure the majority favors.
It narrows a core democratic tool. The citizen initiative was designed to let voters act when their elected officials will not, and the measure raises the bar specifically for that path.
Real recent examples would have failed. Several county special taxes for fire, health, and open space passed with majorities below two-thirds and would not have survived this rule.
The ad valorem provision is easy to overlook. Most coverage focuses on the vote threshold, yet the measure also writes a real property tax limit into the constitution, and its practical reach deserves scrutiny.
6. Open questions
How many recent local special taxes actually passed with between a majority and two-thirds vote, and how much revenue statewide would have been at stake under the new rule?
Does the ad valorem provision in subdivision (b) change anything on the ground, or does it mainly codify limits that courts already enforced?
Will the narrower ACA 22 satisfy the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association over time, or does the withdrawn initiative signal a broader effort to come?
How will the measure interact with the exceptions it cross-references in Article XIII C and Article XIII D, and which taxes fall inside or outside those carve-outs?
With the author now opposed to her own measure, how will the yes and no campaigns be organized and funded?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A special tax funds one specific thing, and the state constitution has long asked for two-thirds approval before a city or county can levy one. Should the same two-thirds rule apply when voters put that tax on the ballot themselves, or should the citizen initiative be a path to a simple-majority tax that elected officials could not pass on their own?
Ask which risk worries you more: A supermajority rule that lets one-third of voters block services the majority wants, or a majority rule that lets an organized campaign commit a community to a targeted tax with less consensus than the constitution otherwise requires?
Learn More About California
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defined as any tax imposed for a specific purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reaffirmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a significant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as different from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s office interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, affirming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratification.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualified an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Office (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fiscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Supporters of Proposition 43 Include:19
• Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association20
• California Taxpayers Association
• California Small Business Association
• Family Business Association of California
• California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
• Reform California21
• California Republican Party
The proponents’ official website is “Yes on 43: Taxpayer
Protection,” https://yesonprop43.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, proponents had raised a total of
$14,856,760.22
Supporters argue that Proposition 43 would:23
• Restore the protections of Prop. 13 (1978) by closing
loopholes created by courts so that local special taxes
must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
• Make it more difficult for special interests to collude with
local governments to impose costly taxes on homeowners,
renters, and small businesses.
• Ensure that taxpayers are in charge by fully protecting their
right to vote on taxes.
• Prevent other rollbacks of Proposition 13.
SUPPORT FOR PROPOSITION 43
Opponents of Proposition 43 Include:24
• California Democratic Party25
• State Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-14)26
• Evolve California27
• Sierra Business Council
• California Professional Firefighters
• Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
• California School Employees Association
• California State Association of Counties
• League of Women Voters of California
• California Teachers Association
The opponents’ official website is “No on 43,”
https://www.noprop43ca.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, opponents had raised a total of
$4,864,393.28
Opponents argue that Proposition 43 would:29
• Threaten funding for parks, affordable housing, firefight-
ing, and other crucial local services that rely on local
revenue.30
• Make it more difficult for cities to secure future revenue
measures.31
• Make California “the hardest place in the country” to raise
local revenue.32
• Undermine majority rule by empowering a minority to
block tax measures favored by a supermajority of voters.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 43
A YES vote for Proposition 43 would increase the threshold
to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives to a two-thirds
majority vote.
A NO vote for Proposition 43 would maintain a simple majority
requirement to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives.

UNDER THE DOME: THE INSIDE STORY ON THE DEAL TO SAVE PROP. 13
Share Page
By Scott Kaufman, Legislative Director
This is the story of how the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association forced the Legislature into a near-unanimous vote to make it harder to raise taxes.
In the last weeks before the Legislature’s summer recess, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association was heavily pressured by special interest groups and elected officials, including the governor’s office, to pull the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 from the November ballot.
Many of our supporters in the business community received even more intense pressure, with demands that they stop helping HJTA’s campaign to pass the initiative. That led to the people concerned about transfer taxes cutting a separate deal for a transfer tax cap, introduced as Assembly Bill 736.
AB 736 was a terrible deal for taxpayers. It was not a constitutional amendment, so its caps on transfer taxes could be overridden with special legislation all the time, like the sales tax cap. And it did nothing at all about closing the “Upland” loophole, ambiguous language in the California Supreme Court’s 2017 California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland decision, which lower courts interpreted to allow special-interest-sponsored “citizens’ initiative tax increases” to evade the two-thirds vote requirement in Proposition 13.
HJTA was pressured to withdraw its initiative for AB 736 alone. But the problem with “Upland” taxes has been getting worse with every election, as more and more interest groups write their own tax increases, direct all the money to themselves, collect signatures to place them on the ballot and then enjoy a much lower vote threshold to pass them than the identical measure would require if placed on the ballot by a government body: 50%-plus-1 instead of 66.67%.
Closing the “Upland” loophole has been a top priority for HJTA for almost 10 years. We cannot save Prop. 13 without closing the “Upland” loophole. We can’t fix transfer taxes without closing the “Upland” loophole. So, despite the pressure to withdraw the initiative in exchange for a transfer tax cap, and threats to spend upwards of $10 million against us if we didn’t, HJTA said no deal.
Then, with just hours to go before the deadline to finalize the ballot, we won a tremendous victory for taxpayers. The governor’s office and the Legislature reversed their previous stance and offered their full support for the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes. They offered to pass a legislative constitutional amendment, Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22, that would close the “Upland” loophole once and for all.
But that wasn’t enough. We also insisted that the Legislature reverse its vote from 2023 that put a “poison pill” constitutional amendment, Assembly Constitutional Amendment 13, on the November ballot. ACA 13 would have required the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 to meet an unusually high vote threshold to pass, potentially making it far more difficult to enact taxpayer protections through the initiative process, permanently.
The governor’s office and the Legislature agreed to our terms. Assembly Constitutional Amendment 21 was passed to remove the poison pill ACA 13 from the November ballot and clear the way for the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 to be approved by a simple majority of voters instead of a more challenging vote threshold. The new measure is exclusively focused on restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes in Proposition 13, after courts have eroded its protections.
That’s the deal to which HJTA agreed as a condition of withdrawing its original initiative.
In exchange, we deferred the fight over transfer taxes to another day, and we gave up the provision in the initiative that would have repealed, in two years, some existing transfer taxes and parcel taxes that court-created loopholes had already allowed.
On June 25, as the clock ticked down to the 5:00 p.m. deadline, the Assembly and the Senate voted almost unanimously to pass two Assembly Constitutional Amendments, ACA 21 and ACA 22, to put the revised Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 on the November ballot and take the poison pill ACA 13 off. HJTA was at the Secretary of State’s office to personally witness the measures being formally enrolled. When they could no longer be revoked, HJTA withdrew the original initiative.
As the legendary comedian W.C. Fields said, “Trust everybody, but cut the cards.”
After the 5:00 p.m. deadline, the Secretary of State officially certified all the November ballot measures. The Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 is now Proposition 43.
When voters approve it, all new local special taxes, those that earmark the revenue for specific purposes, will require a two-thirds vote of the people. This includes transfer taxes, sales taxes, business taxes and parcel taxes. There will no longer be an exception from the two-thirds vote requirement for any “citizens’ initiative tax increases” that were placed on the ballot by special interest groups collecting signatures.
The “Upland” loophole will finally be closed.

#### Vote yes on Prop. 43 to set higher bar for taxes
Re: “Proposition 43 restores voters’ intent on taxes” (Page A6, Oct. 20).
There are a number of ways taxes can be passed.
The California Constitution states that tax proposals not targeted to something specific can pass with 50% + 1 of the voting electorate: aka “general taxes.”
Passing general taxes does not mean that elected officials cannot apply funds to important and beneficial causes, public safety, for example.
Proposals with a specifically targeted purpose require two-thirds (or 66.67%) to pass, as it should be.
More people should be in agreement that yes, Proposition 43 is a worthy cause and vote for it.
...
That is why I am voting yes on Proposition 43.
It does not take away our right to address important, local challenges.
It does make it less easy for elected officials by requiring a higher approval threshold if the issue is deemed to have a very specific purpose.
Vote yes on Proposition 43; do not make it even easier for elected official

Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments

By Sandra Lowe, Special for CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. Below, a city councilmember from Sonoma believes Proposition 43 enables minority rule, making it harder to fund vital government functions. The opposing view: An anti-tax advocate says Prop. 43 solidifies a constitutional amendment passed decades ago that the courts muddied.

Guest Commentary written by

Sometimes things that sound simple are not. 

Let’s take Proposition 43. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments' decisions: majority rule.  

Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority.

Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected.

In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee.

Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. By Susan Shelley, Special for CalMatters

California voters will get to decide in November if it should be harder to pass tax measures at the local level. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes.

California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent state appellate court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.

Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

PUBLISHED: October 3, 2026 at 12:29 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 5, 2026 at 4:13 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Proposition 43 aims to tackle what supporters call a “loophole” in the rules for enacting local tax measures. The system, admittedly, is strange, but it works. We recommend Californians vote no on Prop. 43.
If a city council or a board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax dedicated to a specific purpose such as fire protection or parks, it needs two-thirds of the vote to pass. If, instead, residents put the exact same tax on the ballot by gathering signatures, it needs only a simple majority.
Normally, who is asking should not matter. How much people pay and where the money goes are the same. But it is not that simple. Elected officials face a higher bar, which discourages them from putting every spending wish on the ballot. Residents who organize, qualify a measure and persuade a majority of their voting neighbors to support it have an easier path to fund the things they care about.
Prop. 43 would amend the state constitution to require two-thirds approval for special taxes proposed by residents, the requirement that special taxes proposed by local governments now face. If voters approve it, that change would apply to measures passed after Jan. 1, 2027.
Local tax measures in Sonoma County demonstrate the harm that could follow when little more than one-third of voters can block what most of their neighbors want.
In March 2020, supervisors placed Measure G on the ballot. It asked for a half-cent sales tax for fire services. It received 64.8% support, falling about 2 percentage points short of what it needed to pass. Firefighters and other county residents then gathered nearly 29,000 signatures to place Measure H on the March 2024 ballot. It passed with 61.7% support. Fire agencies have received nearly $46 million, according to their first financial reports.
In November 2024, residents also put Measure I on the ballot. It established a quarter-cent sales tax for child care and children’s health. It passed with nearly 63% support and will raise about $30 million a year.
Neither of those 2024 measures came from elected officials. Residents did the work and put both on the ballot. Under Prop. 43, both would have failed.
This year, Napa County’s Measure B, a citizen-qualified half-cent sales tax for wildfire preparedness, watershed protection and open space, needs only a majority. If it were on the ballot next year and Prop. 43 had passed, it would need two-thirds.
Prop. 43’s supporters argue that they are merely trying to close a “court-created loophole.” The original two-thirds requirement came out of Proposition 13, passed in 1978. However, state courts have concluded that the requirement restrains only local governments because the California Constitution reserves initiative power to the people.
Local councils and boards of supervisors can put a tax measure on the ballot with a vote. One can make a case that the two-thirds requirement serves as a necessary check on that power.
But citizens who seek to put a tax increase or any other measure on the ballot already face significant hurdles, not least gathering thousands of signatures from registered voters. That is not a loophole. It is a system with a real check on each path.
Prop. 43 arrives on the ballot as a political bargain to stave off an even more onerous initiative. It would not cut anyone’s taxes. What it would do is give a minority of voters a veto over funding local services such as parks, fire protection and child care that most of their neighbors want. Ironically, Prop. 43 needs only a simple majority to pass.
Vote no on Prop. 43.

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?

Article continues below this ad
While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

Confused about how to vote on Proposition 43? Here is our endorsement | Opinion
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Thu, September 17, 2026 at 5:30 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.
The SacRT Gold Line light rail line runs along the edge of East Sacramento on June 28, 2025. A half cent sales tax approved by Sacramento County voters provides a reliable funding stream to operate the line. On the November ballot, Proposition 43 seeks to raise the threshold necessary to pass future tax initiatives in California.
Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html) is billed as a taxpayer protection measure that would "save" Proposition 13.
In reality, it would make it much harder for citizen groups in California to pass tax increases to help pay for critical services such as fire and police protection, flood control, health care facilities and road maintenance. It would also make it harder to fund libraries, parks and affordable housing programs that local governments simply can't afford.
Prop. 43 seeks to raise the threshold necessary to pass citizen tax initiatives from a simple majority to a supermajority of 66.7%, which would mean 33.3% of voters would be calling the shots.
THE BEE'S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html)
This is why the combined editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee (https://www.modbee.com/), Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) oppose Prop. 43. We strongly urge a "no" vote.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Prop. 43 would give the minority too much power. It would make it much harder for citizens to take matters into their own hands when governments can't — or won't — finance special projects that serve the public interest.
The ability to pass special taxes is especially important now, when wildfires, droughts and extreme weather leave so many communities vulnerable. Rather than waiting for disaster to strike — or depending on Washington or Sacramento for financial help that may never come — local tax measures can provide revenue to prepare for emergencies, whether it means hiring more firefighters, upgrading equipment or clearing flood channels.
What supporters say
Anti-tax groups, such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (https://www.hjta.org/saveprop13_about_initiative/) andReform California (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/campaigns/stop-the-tax-hikes), say Prop. 43 would merely close a legal loophole used too often by special-interest groups to fund pet projects on the backs of taxpayers.
They say that Proposition 13, which was passed by voters in 1978, specifies that cities, counties and special districts can impose taxes earmarked for specific purposes only with the approval of a supermajority of voters.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Yet language in Prop. 13 and in a follow-up measure, Prop. 218, is somewhat ambiguous. It does not specify that citizen tax initiatives require a supermajority to pass. In a series of court rulings, judges found that they do not.
We weren't convinced by Prop. 43's backers, and voters should be skeptical, too. Nor should they buy into the notion that plenty of money is available if public officials would only stop wasting it on misplaced priorities.
"We can go through any budget, and I will find the cost savings to eliminate the need for a tax increase on any ballot in the state of California this cycle," Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, the head of Reform California, told us.
Never mind that federal and state budget cuts have taken a huge financial toll on local government. Sacramento County, for example, faced a $101 million budget shortfall this year. Atleast half the deficit (https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/cue-web/#/main?uri=https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/webservice/escenic/container/ac765bdc-7f13-11f1-a011-277da135f0d0&mimetype=x-ece/container&extra=%7B%22package%22:%22ece-auto-gen-845e918b-ec6d-4d33-a61b-298f753a3360%22%7D) was attributed to cuts in the federal budget.
Communities rely on special taxes for basic services
Local governments have made foolish and, in some cases, corrupt spending decisions, and they should be held accountable.
Advertisement
Advertisement
But Prop. 43 ignores the fact that many communities have no other way to finance needed services.
Take the tiny community of Crockett, population 3,000, located in Contra Costa County.
Volunteers with the Crockett Improvement Association assumed responsibility for landscaping and maintenance of public spaces — a job that included picking up litter, trimming bushes and maintaining streetlights. But when the work became too onerous for aging volunteers, the group gathered signatures to put a $50-a-year parcel tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Crockett_Community_Services_District,_California,_Measure_L,_Maintenance_and_Landscaping_Tax_Initiative_(November_2022)) on the ballot. It passed by 62.78%.
That's impressive support, yet under Prop. 43, the measure would have failed. Then what? Allow trash and weeds and overgrown bushes to encroach on public spaces?
Advertisement
Advertisement
From a practical standpoint, special taxes are the only way some specific needs can be met, and requiring supermajority approval can create hardships — and even dangers — for communities large and small.
A more reasonable threshold — say 55%, which is the margin required to pass school facility bonds — would be a fair compromise to consider in the future.
For now, voters must decide whether to allow a small minority of voters to dictate whether tax measures should pass. We don't believe they should.

# Your guide to Proposition 43: Voting thresholds for local special taxes
Proposition 43 would clarify that any local special tax on the ballot needs support from two-thirds of voters, rather than a simple majority.
If passed, it would go into effect on Jan. 1.
Local taxes proposed by governments that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
But in recent years, California courts have allowed special taxes proposed by citizens to be approved with a simple majority vote, meaning more than half.

Backers argue that Proposition 43 is needed to close a loophole that makes it easier for groups, including business entities and unions, to seek special taxes.
Opponents contend that raising the threshold will make it harder to pass taxes and a lack of revenue will hurt communities seeking to fix roads or pay for public safety.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 43 would clarify that any local special tax on the ballot needs support from two-thirds of voters, rather than a simple majority. If passed, it would go into effect on Jan. 1.
Local taxes proposed by governments that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. But in recent years, California courts have allowed special taxes proposed by citizens to be approved with a simple majority vote, meaning more than half.
At the same time, the special interests pushing a tax hike are in some cases aligned with politicians on the measure, blurring the line between who is behind a proposed tax increase.
