Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., Family Business Assn. of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce and California Consumer Advocates for Affordability all back the measure. They want to rein in the ability of politicians and special interests to seek higher taxes and argue the cost of living in California is already too high.
Susan Shelley, vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn., argued in a Cal Matters opinion piece (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) that passage of Proposition 43 would clarify existing law.
Advertisement
“There is no ‘citizens’ initiative tax increase exception’ from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up,” she wrote. “Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes.”
One such case is Measure ULA, passed by L.A. voters in 2022. It created a tax on high-value real estate transactions to fund homeless initiatives. The measure passed with 58% of the vote, but opponents argued the two-thirds threshold should have been applied.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> California Professional Firefighters, the California Federation of Teachers, the Nurse Alliance of SEIU California and the California School Employees Assn. all oppose the measure. They argue that it will make it harder to pass tax hikes to pay for police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts.
They also argue that Proposition 43 skirts the California Supreme Court’s opinion on the threshold.
Gubnatorial candidate Xavier Becerra opposes Proposition 43. In a statement, he called corporations “special interests” that want the proposition to pass in order to block new taxes.
Advertisement
“Prop. 43 would hand special interests the power to block the resources our communities count on most: fire protection, safe roads, good schools,” Becerrra said (https://www.noprop43ca.com/news/becerra-announces-opposition-to-proposition-43?source=ec60b1e8-1500-4301-8b7f-6c6ebde9cedd).
Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland), who authored the legislation that became Proposition 43 — ACA 22 — opposes the measure and has urged Californians to vote against it. She said the only reason she crafted the bill was because it was a necessary bargaining chip to torpedo another ballot measure backed by the Jarvis taxpayers group that would have devastated revenues for local governments and retroactively rescinded some local tax increases.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The fight over California tax policy has its roots in Proposition 13 (https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-road-map-proposition-13-baby-boomers-20170709-story.html), the successful 1978 initiative that said local governments couldn’t increase taxes for specific purposes, such as road or school repairs, without the approval of two-thirds of local voters.
California voters also clarified that those taxes included assessments and other fees when they passed Proposition 218 in 1996.
In recent years, private groups seeking to raise local taxes have used voter-backed initiative petitions to get their measures on the ballot.

The California Supreme Court in 2017 indicated that the two-thirds threshold for local taxes applies to measures put on the ballot by elected government bodies, not to those sponsored by citizens.

Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

Prop. 43 Would Make It Harder to Raise Local Taxes. Can It Pass?
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, an anti-tax group who brought California the landmark Proposition 13, is now sponsoring Proposition 43 — a measure to make it harder for cities and counties to raise local taxes.
Aug 18, 2026
Updated Oct 6, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
Close-up of ballot drop box outside of polling place
This November, California voters will consider Proposition 43 — a measure aimed at making it harder for cities and counties to raise local taxes. It’s sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. That’s the anti-tax group that brought California Proposition 13 in 1978, a landmark ballot measure limiting property tax increases.
Marisa sits down with the President of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Jon Coupal. They discuss Prop. 43 and California’s broader tax system.
You can also listen to the Non-Profit Housing Association’s Bill Barnes explain the opposition (https://www.kqed.org/news/12103136/why-opponents-of-prop-43-say-it-would-cripple-local-funding) to Prop. 43.

Why Opponents of Prop. 43 Say It Would Cripple Local Funding
Opponents of Proposition 43 warn that requiring a two-thirds vote for citizen-led special taxes would choke off local revenue as federal funding dries up.
Oct 6, 2026
Updated 5:32 pm PT
Scott Shafer (https://www.kqed.org/author/scottshafer) Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA- MAY 5: In this photo illustration, an official voter information guide mailed to a Southern California resident, ahead of a state primary election, photographed May 5, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo Illustration by Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would raise the requirement for increasing special taxes placed on the ballot by citizens. Right now it takes a simple majority to pass those taxes, but Prop. 43 would require a two-thirds vote.
The initiative is supported by business groups and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. Meanwhile, unions and the California League of Cities say Prop. 43 would cripple their ability to raise critical revenue at a time when the federal government is slashing funding to state and local governments.
Scott and Marisa talk to the No on 43 campaign’s Bill Barnes, who is director of campaigns and community engagement for the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California. Marisa previously discussed the Yes campaign with Jon Coupal (https://www.kqed.org/news/12095893/prop-43-would-make-it-harder-to-raise-local-taxes-can-it-pass), president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.
Don’t forget to use KQED’s voter guide (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide) when filling out your ballot!
Plus, check out Political Breakdown’s weekly newsletter (https://www.kqed.org/newsletters/political-breakdown), delivered straight to your inbox.

5 tax measures are on the California ballot. Here’s how to make sense of them all

In summary
California voters haven’t had to make so many decisions about tax policy at the ballot since 1990. Our analysis shows voters tend to reject new taxes.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
California voters will soon be asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.

Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

43 Two-thirds vote for local special taxes proposed by citizens
Our read Toss-up: majority rule vs. the two-thirds bar
Citizen-proposed local special taxes would need two-thirds, the same bar councils already face. One-third of voters could block what most want.
Share Copy for AI
Markdown (https://www.californiapeople.org/md/prop-43.md)Use with AI agents (https://www.californiapeople.org/ai.html)
Type Legislative constitutional amendment (ACA 22, Wicks)
Sponsor Legislature, as part of a deal with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
Campaign money
$16.4M yes $10.4M no
Your pick
# Key findings
It's a deal to avoid something bigger. Legislative Democrats put this on the ballot so the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association would drop a broader initiative. That one would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority . [1] [2]
Since a 2017 state Supreme Court ruling, citizen-initiated local special taxes have been able to pass by simple majority. LA's mansion tax (Measure ULA, 58% yes in 2022) has generated $1.4B since 2023 , per the city, and Sonoma's 2024 wildfire sales tax passed with 62%. Neither would have passed under Prop 43's threshold. [1] [3]
It isn't retroactive, so ULA and similar taxes stay [1] . It applies to new, increased or extended citizen taxes from Jan 1, 2027. [3]
Yes $16.4M (business and property-owner committee $15.5M, HJTA committee $0.85M). No $10.4M , $7.8M of it through a labor-sponsored committee. Through Oct 22, 2026. [4]
# Track record
Year
Event
Effect
1996
Prop 218
Special taxes placed by local governments need two-thirds
2017
State Supreme Court ruling
Citizen-initiated special taxes now need only a majority [5]
2022
LA Measure ULA
58% yes; $1.4B generated since 2023
2024
Sonoma County wildfire and emergency services sales tax
62% yes
2026
Prop 43
Two-thirds for citizen special taxes from 2027 on
[3] [2]
# Money and conflicts
The Yes money comes from business and property-owner groups, and most No money from labor [4] . Unions and advocates would lose a tool they've used to pass local taxes by majority.
The Legislature traded this for HJTA dropping a broader measure. Its author, Asm. Buffy Wicks, says she is "adamantly opposed" to Prop 43. [1] That deal is done: the HJTA measure is off the ballot whether Prop 43 passes or fails, so the deal is not a reason to vote either way.
# Does it solve a lasting problem?
It makes the rule the same whether a tax comes from a city council or a petition, and it ends a workaround. It also lets one-third of voters block taxes most voters support. ULA is the test case for both sides: it raised real money, and the evidence on construction is contested. A UCLA Lewis Center study (corrected in 2026) finds a 31% drop in permits for 20-plus-unit projects in LA County; an Occidental College reanalysis finds no meaningful change and attributes the shift to interest rates. [6] [7]
# If you vote yes: accountability
Bottom line: Starting Jan 1, 2027, a special tax (one with a set purpose) proposed by citizens would need a two-thirds vote, the same bar that already applies when a city council or county board proposes one. [3] Voters lose the majority-vote route that court rulings opened. Taxes that already passed that way stay. [1]
# Who's accountable
Your city council and county board of supervisors still decide which taxes they put on the ballot, and under what rules.
County registrars and city clerks run local elections and report which vote threshold applies to each measure.
# What to watch
Fights over how a measure is labeled, since a "special" tax needs two-thirds and other kinds don't.
Whether groups that used citizen initiatives for local taxes, like LA's mansion tax, shift to other approaches. [1]
# Public records to request (CPRA)
Anyone can file a California Public Records Act request (the state's version of FOIA), with no reason required. Agencies must respond within 10 days, or 24 in unusual cases. [9] For any local tax measure, ask your city clerk or county registrar for the petition, the official title and summary, and any legal opinion on which vote threshold applies.
What it does
New, increased or extended local special taxes proposed by citizen initiative need two-thirds starting Jan 1, 2027. [3]
Fiscal effect: local revenue may grow more slowly; the size is unknown. [3]
What we're not asking
The workaround survives. Courts allow a majority-vote general tax paired with a non-binding advisory measure on how to spend it (Johnson v. County of Mendocino, 2018). Prop 43 pushes citizen groups toward that: taxes with no legal earmark, which is less accountable, not more. [8]
Who's affected: ULA-style transfer taxes, wildfire and sales taxes like Sonoma's, and future transit or homelessness measures. [1]
ULA's lesson is contested: a 31% drop in large-project permits (UCLA, corrected 2026) vs. no meaningful change (Occidental). [6] [7]
Game theory. HJTA got its deal, business groups fund the campaign, labor loses a tool, and both sides return in 2028 with the next initiative. The Legislature's own tax measures aren't affected.
Better or worse? One rule for council and citizen taxes vs. a one-third veto and a push toward unearmarked taxes.
Open questions: How many citizen special taxes passed with 50–66% since 2017? The LAO gives no count.
Both sides
For: HJTA, Reform California, Southern California News Group, SD Union-Tribune. It stops special interests from passing taxes in low-turnout elections. [2]
Against: CA Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000, Sacramento Bee. It lets moneyed interests block tax initiatives most voters support. [2]

California's Proposition 43 is asking voters to require a two-thirds vote for local special taxes that residents place on the ballot by petition.
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local special tax that residents place on the ballot by petition, the same threshold that already applies when a city council, county board or special district proposes one. A special tax is one whose money is dedicated to a specific purpose, such as fire protection, parks, housing or schools. Since a series of court rulings that began in 2017, voter-proposed special taxes have needed only a simple majority. Prop 43 would end that for measures approved from January 1, 2027, and it leaves every tax already on the books in place.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Prop 43 is a legislative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/) (ACA 22) that the Legislature placed on the ballot on June 25 as part of a deal with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which withdrew a broader initiative the same day. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it trails in both public polls that have tested it: 43% yes and 51% no in PPIC's September survey, and 31% yes, 40% no in UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies poll. This explainer covers what the text does, the court rulings it responds to, the taxes that passed under the majority rule, the deal that produced it, what the Legislative Analyst's Office says it costs, and who is paying for each side.
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote for voter-proposed local special taxes:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a single section, 4.5, to Article XIII A of the California Constitution, the article voters created with Proposition 13 in 1978. Its first subdivision reads: "Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax" unless it is "submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote."
Three parts of that sentence do the work:
"Including the electorate … exercising the initiative power." These words bring residents who propose a tax by petition under the same rule as the officials who govern them. Article II is the article that grants the initiative power, and the "notwithstanding" clause sets it aside for this purpose.
"Impose, extend, or increase." The rule covers new taxes, higher rates and renewals. A voter-proposed special tax that passed by majority before 2027 keeps running, but extending it past its end date or raising its rate would need two-thirds.
"Special tax." The measure borrows its definitions from Article XIII C, the article added by Proposition 218 in 1996: a special tax is one "imposed for specific purposes," and a "local government" is any county, city, city and county, including a charter city or county, any special district, or any other local or regional governmental entity. General taxes, whose money can be spent on anything, still pass by majority no matter who proposes them.
A second subdivision states that no local government, "including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property," except the property tax Article XIII D already allows. The Legislative Analyst's Office does not discuss this clause as a separate change, and neither ballot argument mentions it.
The Attorney General's summary puts the timing plainly: the measure "applies to voter-proposed ballot measures approved after January 1, 2027." Local tax measures on the November 3 ballot are still decided under the current rules.
California's local special taxes follow two vote thresholds today, depending on who proposes them:
Under the State Constitution, a special tax that a local government places on the ballot needs two-thirds of the vote. That rule dates to Proposition 13 and was restated in Proposition 218. For decades it was widely assumed to apply to every special tax. The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm) describes the change in one line: "recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are proposed by voters to be approved with a majority vote."
The first of those decisions was not about the vote threshold at all. In California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (August 28, 2017), the California Supreme Court considered a local initiative that would have allowed three medical marijuana dispensaries in Upland and charged each $75,000 a year. The court held that Proposition 218's requirement to hold general-tax elections at a regularly scheduled general election "applies only to local governments and not to the electorate's initiative power without evidence that such was the intended purpose of the requirement," as a 2018 legislative hearing paper (https://arev.assembly.ca.gov/sites/arev.assembly.

The court added a test for future cases: "Without a direct reference in the text of a provision—or a similarly clear, unambiguous indication that it was within the ambit of a provision's purpose to constrain the people's initiative power—we will not construe a provision as imposing such a limitation."
Appellate courts then applied that reasoning to special taxes. In June 2020 the First District Court of Appeal upheld San Francisco's November 2018 Proposition C, a business tax for homelessness services, reading the two-thirds requirements "as coexisting with, not displacing, the people's power to enact initiatives by majority vote." The Fifth District reached the same result for Fresno's parks tax in December 2020. The First District did so again in 2021 for two more San Francisco measures, a June 2018 commercial rent tax for child care and a parcel tax for teacher pay (https://cases.justia.com/california/court-of-appeal/2021-a160659.pdf), noting that every appellate court to address the question had agreed. The California Supreme Court declined to review the ruling on the child care tax, which had passed with about 51%, according to the San Francisco City Attorney (https://sfcityattorney.org/?p=8889).
Prop 43 answers that test in its own words. Its text names "the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power," the kind of "direct reference" the Upland court said a limit on voters would require.
Local special taxes today vs Proposition 43 and the withdrawn initiative:
Rule Today If Proposition 43 passes Withdrawn initiative #1983 (for comparison)
Special tax placed on the ballot by a city council, board or district Two-thirds vote Two-thirds vote (no change) Two-thirds vote
Special tax placed on the ballot by citizen petition Majority vote, under 2020 and 2021 appellate rulings Two-thirds vote, for measures from January 1, 2027 Two-thirds vote
General tax (money for any purpose) Majority vote Majority vote (no change) Majority vote
Special taxes already passed by majority (Measure ULA, Fresno Measure P and others) Stay in effect Stay in effect; any later extension or increase needs two-thirds Existing property-related special taxes passed below two-thirds voided two years after enactment
Charter-city real estate transfer taxes Allowed at rates each city sets Not addressed Banned beyond the statewide documentary transfer tax, including existing ones
Legislative Analyst's fiscal estimate Not applicable Local tax revenue "could be lower in the future"; amount "unknown" Annual loss of "up to a couple of billion dollars," mostly in charter cities
Four voter-initiated special taxes passed with 52% to 61%, all short of two-thirds:
The taxes that passed under the majority rule include some of the largest local revenue measures of the past decade. Four with public records of both their vote share and their citizen-initiative status:
San Francisco Proposition C (November 2018) , a gross receipts tax on large businesses for homelessness services, passed with 61.34% of 351,326 votes, according to the Court of Appeal's opinion (https://cases.justia.com/california/court-of-appeal/2020-a158645.pdf).
San Francisco Proposition G (June 2018) , a parcel tax for San Francisco Unified School District teacher pay, passed with 60.76% of 238,133 votes.
Fresno Measure P (November 2018) , a 30-year sales tax for parks estimated at $37.5 million a year, passed with 52.17%. The city first declared it failed for lack of two-thirds and then certified it as passed in February 2021 after the appellate ruling, according to the Fresno City Council's legislative file (https://agendas.fresno.gov/en/legislation/id-21-344-12830).
Los Angeles Measure ULA (November 2022) , known as the "mansion tax," adds a 4% tax on sales of real property over $5 million and 5.5% on sales of $10 million or more, "until ended by voters." It passed with 512,808 votes to 374,934, or 57.77%, according to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder (https://results.lavote.gov/). Under a two-thirds rule it would have needed 591,828 yes votes, 79,020 more than it received. The Los Angeles Housing Department (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula) says collections began April 1, 2023, with 70% of the money going to affordable housing and 30% to homelessness prevention. CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-prop-43-election-2026/) that the thresholds, indexed to inflation, now stand at $5.3 million and $10.6 million and that the city says the tax has raised $1.4 billion.
Proposition 43's two-thirds threshold is sitting above four voter-initiated special taxes in San Francisco, Fresno and Los Angeles that passed with 52% to 61% of the vote between 2018 and 2022. Other measures followed the same path. CalMatters reports that 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax for wildfire response and emergency services in 2024, short of two-thirds. Neither campaign nor the LAO publishes a statewide count of voter-initiated special taxes passed by majority since 2017, so these examples are not a complete list.
None of these taxes would be repealed. Prop 43 applies from 2027 forward. What would change is the next one: a new citizen-proposed parcel tax, sales tax or transfer tax, or a renewal or increase of an existing one, would need two-thirds.
Proposition 43 came from a June 25 deal that replaced a broader Howard Jarvis initiative:
Prop 43 is the narrow survivor of a much larger fight. In 2024 the California Supreme Court unanimously removed the Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act, which would have raised the thresholds for approving local taxes among other changes, from that year's ballot, ruling it an invalid revision of the Constitution rather than an amendment, the law firm Hanson Bridgett reported (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publication/240620-4000-ca-supreme-court-bars-fall-ballot-measure). The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association then qualified a new initiative for 2026, the "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13" (initiative #1983, A.G. file 25-0006). Its petition drive was paid for by Protect Prop. 13, a project of the association, according to the Secretary of State's top-funders filing (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/1983-top-funders-01-05-26.pdf).
That initiative went much further than Prop 43. It would have required two-thirds for voter-proposed special taxes, barred charter cities from imposing real estate transfer taxes beyond the statewide documentary transfer tax, and overturned existing property-related taxes that did not meet those rules two years after passage. The LAO's 2025 analysis (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) estimated an "annual loss of revenues to local governments totaling up to a couple of billion dollars, predominantly affecting certain charter cities." That included about $300 million a year in existing parcel taxes approved with less than two-thirds, and the special-purpose transfer taxes that voters "recently" approved in Los Angeles and Santa Monica. Measure ULA was one of them.
The Legislature had its own measure on the 2026 ballot aimed at that initiative. ACA 13, passed in 2023, would have required any initiative that raises a vote threshold to pass by that same higher threshold, which in practice meant two-thirds for the Howard Jarvis measure.
Both came off the ballot on June 25, the last day an initiative could be withdrawn. The deal was announced by the initiative's proponents, Governor Gavin Newsom and legislative leaders, according to the California Special Districts Association (https://www.csda.net/blogs/morgan-leskody/2026/06/29/legislature-cuts-deal-with-vote-threshold-proponen). That day:
ACA 21 (Resolution Chapter 131) removed ACA 13 from the November ballot, according to the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures).
ACA 22 (Resolution Chapter 132), by Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, an Oakland Democrat, was introduced and adopted by both houses without committee hearings, according to the legislative record mirrored on LegiScan (https://legiscan.com/CA/bill/ACA22/2025). It passed the Assembly 68–2 and the Senate 35–1 and became Prop 43.
Jon Coupal , the association's president, withdrew initiative #1983 under Elections Code section 9604, according to a Secretary of State memo to county elections officials (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26167jh.pdf).
"Today the Legislature voted to make it harder to raise taxes," Coupal said (https://www.hjta.org/press-releases/taxpayers-win-in-sacramento-with-unprecedented-support-for-two-thirds-vote-requirement-to-raise-special-taxes/) in a joint release with the California Taxpayers Association. Wicks wrote the compromise language and days later said she was "adamantly opposed" to it, CalMatters reported. Her explanation, in a social media post the outlet quoted: "The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy."
LAO fiscal estimate says local tax revenue could be lower, by an unknown amount:
The LAO's analysis of Prop 43 is short. Because the measure "makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes," it says, "local governments' tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters." The ballot summary of the fiscal effect reads: "Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes."
The estimate has no dollar figure because Prop 43 touches no existing tax. Its effect depends on how many voter-proposed special taxes would win between 50% and 66.7% of the vote in future elections.
Proposition 43's Yes campaign reports $14.0 million from its top donors and the No side $6.7 million:
The Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 14, shows $14.0 million from the ten largest donors to the Yes committee, "Yes on Prop 43 – The Local Taxpayer Protection Act." The California Business Roundtable Issues PAC gave $9.87 million; the FPPC lists Peter Thiel and Kim DeGeorge as its top donors. Protect Prop. 13, the Howard Jarvis project, gave $1.04 million, and the real estate companies Kilroy Realty and Douglas Emmett Properties gave $1 million each.
The No committee, "No on Prop 43: Stop the Local Taxpayer Deception Act," reports $5.6 million from its ten largest donors. The SEIU California State Council gave $1.5 million. The California Teachers Association, two carpenters' councils, two SEIU locals, the Southern California Partnership for Jobs and the California Alliance for Jobs gave $500,000 each. The California Professional Firefighters gave $365,257, and the League of California Cities' CITIPAC gave $250,000. A third committee formed for several measures, Communities for an Affordable California (Yes on 3, No on 39 and 43), adds $1.09 million, which brings the FPPC's opposition total to $6.7 million. The FPPC marks that last figure with an asterisk because, for a committee covering more than one measure, "it is not possible to determine the amount of the contribution that was spent specifically on the campaign for any particular measure."
The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-43-aca-22-wicks-local-taxes-limitation-res-ch-132-2026), which counts all reported contributions through October 6 rather than the largest donors, shows $10.0 million for the two Yes committees and $8.0 million for the two committees opposing it. The Million Voters Project's committee also opposes Proposition 39 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/yes-voter-id-laws-are-on-the-california-ballot-proposition-39s-rules-costs-and-court-fights/) and supports Proposition 3 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-millionaire-tax-proposition-3/).
The arguments over Proposition 43 pit "closing loopholes" against "minority rule":
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by the presidents of the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, says "court decisions created loopholes that allow special interests to impose massive new tax increases by circumventing the taxpayer protections voters approved." It says local governments "have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade" and that "some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%," which on a $900,000 home "would cost a homeowner $54,000 simply for selling their house." The argument does not say how many of those 2,000 taxes were voter-proposed special taxes, the only kind Prop 43 affects. The rebuttal, signed by Coupal and others, calls the Legislature's vote "nearly unanimous" and says it shows "activist courts exceeded voters' intent."
The No argument, signed by the presidents of the California Professional Firefighters and the California School Employees Association and the executive director of SEIU's Nurse Alliance, says Prop 43 "makes it harder for you to fund critical services like police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff our local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts." Its central objection is arithmetic: the measure lets "just over one-third of voters" block "what nearly 67% want," and "makes their NO vote count twice as much as a YES vote." It says "corporate donors who spend big in elections will benefit most." The No rebuttal adds that Prop 43 "doesn't cut your taxes a penny."
The campaigns' claims go beyond the guide. The No campaign's release of Governor Newsom's statement says communities "would have lost nearly $3 billion a year" if Prop 43 had been law, a figure the LAO does not estimate. The guide notes that ballot arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Proposition 43 trails in both public polls, and Governor Newsom opposes it:
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 43% yes, 51% no and 6% undecided. Republicans support it 61% to 35%. Democrats oppose it 60% to 33%, and independents 51% to 43%. Homeowners split 48% yes to 47% no, while renters oppose it 61% to 33%. Only 1% named it the measure they were most interested in. UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies, polling September 15–20, found 31% yes and 40% no, with the rest undecided.
Governor Newsom, who took part in announcing the June deal, now opposes the measure. "This dangerous corporate power grab would let big corporations avoid paying their fair share and threaten billions in funding for critical services like 911 response and wildfire prevention. Vote NO on 43," he said in a statement the No campaign released (https://www.noprop43ca.com/news/statement-governor-newsom-announces-opposition-to-proposition-43) on October 9. Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor, announced his opposition on September 9. The California Democratic Party opposes (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 43, and the California Republican Party supports (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it.
The Voter Information Guide lists the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce in support, with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association as the Yes campaign's contact. Opponents listed in the No argument are the California Professional Firefighters, Californians Against Waste, the California Federation of Teachers, the California School Employees Association, Communities for a Better Environment, AAPI Force, the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California, the Nurse Alliance of SEIU California and the Sierra Business Council. The Bay Area planning group SPUR recommends (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-43-local-tax-threshold) a no vote. The editorial boards we found have all recommended against it: the Santa Rosa Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/03/endorsement-prop-43-wants-to-fix-a-system-that-isnt-broken/) (October 3), the Santa Barbara Independent (https://www.independent.com/2026/10/07/the-santa-barbara-independent-endorsements-for-the-general-election-november-3-2026/) (October 7) and the Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article316956235.html).
Proposition 43 after November 3 would mean a two-thirds rule from 2027 or no change to majority rule:
If Prop 43 passes, it takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State certifies the results, which is due December 11, and its two-thirds rule applies to voter-proposed special taxes approved from January 1, 2027. Measure ULA, Fresno's parks tax, San Francisco's Propositions C and G, and every other tax already approved would stay in force, but a renewal or increase of any of them would need two-thirds. Campaigns for new local taxes could still pass a general tax by majority. If it fails, the court-made rule stands: residents who gather signatures can pass a special tax with a simple majority, while councils and boards still need two-thirds. Either way, the broader Howard Jarvis initiative will not be on this ballot. It was withdrawn under the June deal.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, campaign-finance data as of October 14, 2026 (FPPC) and October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State), party positions as of October 12, 2026, and polling fielded through September 20, 2026.

Prop
43
CA
Prop
43
|
Constitutional Amendment
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
Requires two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes, specifically eliminating the ability for a citizen initiative to qualify with a simple majority vote.
SPUR's Recommendation
SPUR has consistently called for reforming Prop. 13 and opposed onerous new restrictions on the government’s ability to raise needed revenue. Prop. 43 would take the state in the opposite direction. The measure would cement and expand Prop. 13's legacy by amending the California Constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for imposing or extending any special tax. It would undermine both the democratic principle of majority rule and one of the few remaining pathways for funding important services.
Vote NO
What Prop. 43 Would Do
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote of the electorate to approve all special taxes, whether placed on the ballot through citizen initiative (voter signatures) or by government officials.
Proposition 13 in 1978 amended the California constitution to limit local governments’ ability to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) by requiring a minimum two-thirds approval by voters. In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that taxes placed on the ballot by voters through signature gathering were not subject to this same two-thirds requirement. Prop. 43 seeks to overturn the 2017 decision and amend the constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval requirement for any new, extended, or increased local special tax, regardless of whether the initiative was placed on the ballot by local government officials or through a voter initiative.
The Backstory
Prop. 43 is the latest proposal in a decades-long series of amendments to the California Constitution that have significantly limited local governments' ability to fund projects and services by imposing new taxes. In 1978, Prop. 13 capped property tax rates at 1% of assessed value and established the initial two-thirds voter requirement to approve special taxes. In 2017, however, the California Supreme Court clarified in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (Upland) that many of the key provisions in the California Constitution restricting the imposition of new taxes applied only to proposals put forward by the government. Consequently, the Upland decision established that new special tax measures submitted through citizen initiative required only a 50% plus one vote majority to pass rather than two-thirds approval. 1 Since that decision, a number of local special taxes in California have passed with a simple majority after being placed on the ballot through voter initiative. Such measures account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide.
Prop. 43 would establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for new special taxes regardless of how they were placed on the ballot. The California Legislature placed the proposition on the ballot after reaching a compromise with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, which had another, similar proposal to amend the California Constitution. 2 That proposal had qualified for the November 2026 ballot through a voter signature-gathering campaign. The compromise sidelines some of the more complex issues in the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association’s proposed amendment and instead offers a simplified amendment focused only on the voter threshold.
Prop. 43 requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 43 would make it significantly more difficult to raise revenues for local government services and projects by requiring a higher approval threshold. It is likely that the resulting fiscal impacts to government, in the form of unfunded programs or expiring taxes that can no longer be renewed, would fall most heavily on lower-income residents and people of color. In the Bay Area, for example, the citizen initiative process has recently been used to propose taxes to support transit operations and has been discussed as a potential future pathway to place a regional affordable housing bond before the voters. Transit operations and affordable housing are both examples of government expenditures that disproportionately benefit lower-income residents and people of color and that will be difficult to sustain without viable approaches to securing new revenues.
Additionally, placing broad restrictions on how the electorate can raise taxes can drive the government to seek other, less equitable sources of revenue. The severe limitations Prop. 13 placed on property taxes, for example, have, among other factors, helped drive local governments to increasingly rely on sales taxes, a much more regressive revenue source.
Pros
Prop. 43 would simplify existing law and establish a consistent, uniform voter threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing new special taxes.
The measure would maintain the 50% plus one vote threshold for passing general taxes (those not dedicated to a specific purpose).
Cons
Prop. 43 would undermine the basic principle of majority rule by imposing a heightened approval threshold on certain voter-proposed initiatives.
The measure would continue and expand on the legacy of Prop. 13, a law that has profoundly distorted California’s tax structure, fueled wealth inequality, and exacerbated the state’s housing challenges by disincentivizing home sales and turnover.
It would eliminate one of the few viable ways to raise local revenues at a time when local governments' fiscal needs are especially acute.

Proposition 43, sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, may seem pretty basic. It is a constitutional amendment that would restore the two-thirds vote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) requirement to enact all local “special taxes” intended to fund a specific, designated purpose, such as public safety or libraries.
But the ballot measure is more accurately seen as Howard Jarvis giving voters a chance to tell the California Supreme Court to take a hike — to stop sabotaging popular state laws that create obstacles to newer and higher taxes. Just as Republican-appointed U.S. Supreme Court justices tailor their legal rulings to meet broad conservative objectives, some of the state supremes’ most important rulings feel contrived to achieve the goals of the liberal Sacramento establishment.
An obvious example is the court’s contrary rulings on citizen initiatives, which have long since lost their noble patina of being a way for voters to use “direct democracy” to overcome special interests. Instead, as political scientists and journalists have documented for decades, such measures are routinely stage-managed (https://digitalcommons.lmu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3172&context=llr) by powerful forces — unions, business organizations and, yes, elected officials.
Sometimes the state’s justices choose to ignore this history. Sometimes they emphasize it.
In a 2017 case involving a ballot measure related to cannabis dispensaries in the city of Upland, the court, on a 5-2 vote, drastically changed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) how the judicial system interpreted voter-approved state laws, especially Proposition 13 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)) — the landmark 1978 legislation that kicked off a national taxpayer rights movement. The majority held that since the measure reached the ballot because of a citizen signature-gathering campaign — instead of the direct action of a local government body — simple majority support was necessary for enactment, not the two-thirds vote specified in Proposition 13.
Why? Because, per Justice Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar, courts must “liberally construe the public’s statewide and local initiative power.” Yet it was literally undisputed that the Upland measure reached the ballot not because of a backlash to City Hall machinations from residents but because of a well-funded effort by a cannabis trade group.
But in 2018, the state high court unanimously agreed (https://www.rstreet.org/commentary/public-sector-unions-win-big-at-the-california-supreme-court-in-getting-san-diego-pension-reforms-overturned/) that a 2012 ballot measure approved by a huge majority of San Diegans that ended defined benefit pensions for most new city hires should be invalidated (https://www.rstreet.org/commentary/public-sector-unions-win-big-at-the-california-supreme-court-in-getting-san-diego-pension-reforms-overturned/). Why? Because the fact that 116,000 city residents signed the petitions to put the measure on the ballot was tainted by the strong support of then-Mayor Jerry Sanders, who was depicted as trying to get around laws that require the city to collectively bargain changes in employment terms.
What he was trying to get around was the fact that the City Council majority, allied with unions, bitterly opposed pension changes despite compensation costs eating up a massive and growing chunk of city budgets. As former City Attorney Jan Goldsmith wrote (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2012/02/29/initiative-process-is-first-power-reserved-to-the-people/), “Never in the history of California has there ever been a requirement to negotiate with labor unions over terms of a citizens’ initiative placed on the ballot by voter signatures.”
These rulings can’t be squared. The state Supreme Court treats the citizen initiative process as a sacrosanct part of state government that must be “liberally construed” when it comes to allowing tax hikes on a simple majority vote. But when it comes to a campaign to contain pension costs, it is collective bargaining laws that must be “liberally construed” — not “the public’s statewide and local initiative power.”
Perhaps this background won’t make much difference to voters with one of two basic, contrary opinions: “It needs to be difficult to raise taxes in California” and “It shouldn’t take supermajorities to raise taxes.” But we raise a third crucial consideration: Checks and balances are essential to government — whether in r

FILE – In this June 7, 1978 file photo, Paul Gann, left, and Howard Jarvis, right, celebrate as their co-authored tax initiative Proposition 13 takes a commanding lead and ultimately won in the California primary in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/File)
By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: August 9, 2026 at 9:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: August 28, 2026 at 12:16 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
On the California Secretary of State’s website describing qualified statewide measures for the November ballot, voters will see a three-word reference to Proposition 43 referring to “Local taxes: limitation.” (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures) It’s ironic the initiative that has sparked the most backroom drama in years is depicted with such little fanfare.
Prop. 43 was placed on the ballot by a panicked California Legislature after a last- minute deal was struck with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to pull the association’s more sweeping Local Taxpayer Protection Act from the ballot. Despite the complicated inside-the-Capitol machinations with lobbyists and lawmakers, the resulting measure is rather simple.
If voters approve it, Prop. 43 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/aca-22.pdf) would close a court created loophole that allowed some local special taxes to evade the two-thirds vote requirement — taxes for specific items such as transit, housing, flood control and parks. Specifically, tax increases that are placed on the ballot by citizens via signature-gathering.
This change would restore the threshold to the design of 1978’s tax-limiting Proposition 13. Since then, a series of bone-headed court decisions (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/courts-widen-the-door-to-even-more-local-taxes-in-california/) determined that voters could approve citizen-driven special tax increases by a simple majority, while maintaining the two-thirds rule for special tax increases directly placed on the ballot by local governments. This loophole led to abuses, as unions served as the cat’s paw for local officials by gathering signatures to place tax increases on the ballot and pass them with less than a two-thirds vote.
So, the bottom line: Vote yes on Proposition 43, as it will impede local governments from getting around the two-thirds vote for special taxes to bail themselves out of endless budget debacles. As the economy has stumbled and local governments have burned through “free” COVID money from Washington, D.C., municipalities increasingly are turning to bonds and tax increases (https://caltax.org/2026/03/20/voters-to-decide-fate-of-80-local-tax-and-bond-measures-in-june/) .
Money is fungible. If voters approve “special” (https://flooddistrict.marincounty.gov/question/what-is-a-special-tax/) taxes, that leaves more money in the general fund to spend as usual. That typically means bigger paychecks and pensions for powerful public-employee unions. The two-thirds vote threshold is one of the few ways that California taxpayers can at least try to force their elected officials to live within their means.
That said, we’re disappointed that the final measure doesn’t include a ban and rollback of local transfer taxes. For instance, Los Angeles’ disastrous “mansion tax” (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2025-10-01/apartment-development-pipeline-dries-up-in-spite-of-demand-for-housing) not only imposes astronomical rates on Angelenos who sell pricey homes (currently a 4% tax on homes priced above $5.4 million and 5.5% on those priced above $10.9 million) — but applies to apartment and commercial properties. Predictably, that has quashed housing production in Los Angeles.

The original initiative by HJTA banned real estate transfer taxes above a minor documentary transfer fee. Proponents ultimately pulled that initiative from the ballot at the last minute after the Legislature passed the compromise (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) measure that deals only with the two-thirds vote issue. The Legislature also agreed to pull a separate ballot measure designed to make it harder to pass all future tax-limitation efforts, including this one. This deal to remove the transfer-tax portion of the initiative led to a split within the business coalition that had supported it.
Complicating matters further, the key Democratic lawmakers who placed the current measure on the ballot are calling for voters to reject it. They placed it there simply as a means to derail something that they viewed as far worse (https://sdvoice.info/on-your-november-ballot-proposition-43/) because it protected taxpayers even more from the predations of government and allied special interests. But voters needn’t get caught up in the back story, however interesting as insight into Sacramento’s sausage-making process.
As it stands, the final measure is praiseworthy, as it puts the brakes on local governments’ ability to collude with special interests to more easily raise your taxes. Vote yes on Prop. 43 to make it harder to raise taxes.

As voting begins in this election season, it is a good time to start considering some of the more egregious lies being foisted on voters in campaign ads, editorials and op-eds.
Let’s start with what is being represented about Proposition 43, the effort to close a court-created loophole in Proposition 13. Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Prop. 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes and parcel taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters.
Note what Prop. 43 does not do. It does not cut any local taxes. It does not retroactively invalidate any existing tax. It does not limit any local governments from going to the voters for general tax increases, which pass with a simple majority vote. All that it does is restore the two-thirds vote for local special taxes – taxes imposed for a specific purpose.
Despite the negligible impact Prop. 43 would have on existing local government revenues, according to critics, Prop. 43 will result in the end of civilization. In an op-ed in the San Jose Mercury News, the president of California Professional Firefighters, Darrell Roberts, claims that Prop. 43 “would place a nearly insurmountable roadblock from placing any measure on the ballot” to impose a special tax. What Mr. Roberts forgets is that the two-thirds vote for local special taxes was a provision of the California Constitution from 1978 until 2017 when the California courts began crafting an exception. During that time, rather than being an “insurmountable” barrier, special taxes were routinely enacted with the requisite two-thirds vote, including sales taxes and parcel taxes.
The argument that supermajority vote requirements are somehow “undemocratic” collapses when one considers the long history of America’s constitutional framework. There are no fewer than twelve instances in the U.S. Constitution requiring a two-thirds vote. These include impeachment; expelling a Member of Congress; overriding a veto; amending the Constitution (Congressional approval of a Joint Resolution proposing an amendment to the U.S. Constitution requires a 2/3 majority); calling a Constitutional Convention; and ratifying a treaty.
Here in California, the two-thirds vote requirement on matters related to taxation dates back to 1879. That was when the higher threshold was placed in the state constitution for local general obligation bonds as a protection against excessive debt at the local level, repaid by property owners. Recently, in the November 2024 election, California voters overwhelmingly rejected an effort to lower the two-thirds vote requirement for most local bonds to 55%. Prop. 5 lost by ten points.
What is revealing about the opposition to Prop. 43 is that most is coming from public sector labor organizations – the very interests who want to remove all barriers to higher taxes.
Hyperbolic support for tax increases is prevalent throughout the local level of government as well. Although not a statewide measure, a proposal to raise the sales taxes in five Bay Area counties to generate billions for failed transit systems has driven proponents of the tax to near madness in describing the parade of horribles if the tax fails in November. But this “Regional Transit Measure” has weak support notwithstanding a well-funded campaign to promote it. Voters are suspicious because the transit districts in question, especially BART, have done nothing to correct their failures and inefficiencies. Not surprisingly, Bay Area residents want at least some proof that the new revenue won’t be as misspent as existing revenue.
Despite the track record of waste and fraud, major Bay Area media outlets are fully in support of increasing sales taxes, which everyone admits are very regressive. The San Francisco Chronicle warns that, “without an immediate infusion of funds, Muni could be forced to cut service by at least 30%, cancel at least 20 bus routes, end regular evening service, eliminate cable car service and reduce fare discounts for vulnerable populations. BART could close 15 stations and reduce service by 70%. Caltrain could reduce service to one train per hour and stop service on weekends.”
The organization Fixes Before Funding disputes these dire predictions, noting, “Transit costs and subsidies have exploded while service shrank; when ridership and fare revenue collapsed, the agencies did not restructure; spending per rider has gone off the chart; ridership never recovered, and never grew the way planners promised; and, the signature projects ran over budget and under-delivered.”
A great deal of overstatement can be expected in any political contest, but when it comes to the predictions of disaster if more taxes are not forthcoming, voters would be well advised to ignore the hype.
Jon Coupal is president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
